primary-sector.def: The part of the economy that takes resources straight from nature: farming, fishing, forestry and mining.

secondary-sector.def: The part of the economy that turns raw materials into goods, such as factories and building.

tertiary-sector.def: The part of the economy that provides services, such as shops, transport, health care and teaching. Also called the service sector.

quaternary-sector.def: The part of the service economy that creates and moves information, such as research, software and finance.

quinary-sector.def: The part of the service economy where the highest-level decisions are made, by top officers of big firms and governments.

break-of-bulk.def: A place where goods are moved from one kind of transport to another, such as from ships to trains at a port. Processing plants often cluster there.

least-cost-theory.def: A model that says a factory locates where its total costs of transport, labor and nearby firms are lowest. Weight-losing industries locate near raw materials, weight-gaining ones near markets.

core.def: In world-system terms, the countries with mostly high-wage service, research and decision jobs and advanced industry. A model category, not an official list.

semiperiphery.def: In world-system terms, countries between the core and the periphery, with a large factory sector and growing services. A model category, not an official list.

periphery.def: In world-system terms, countries where many people do primary-sector and low-wage work, often exporting raw materials. A model category, not an official list.
